planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Set divisions into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, spacing plants to allow the tidy clumps to knit together over a season or two. Morning Star forms a compact mound of deeply cut, star-shaped leaves brushed with burgundy along the veins, staying neater and less sprawling than many stoloniferous foamflowers. In mid-spring numerous slender stems carry soft pink, star-shaped flowers well above the foliage for a long-lasting display. Keep the shallow roots consistently moist and mulched, and divide congested clumps in spring or fall every few years to renew vigor.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade and give it room to run, since Oregon Trail spreads rapidly by surface stolons into a fast-filling, semi-evergreen groundcover mat. The deeply lobed, well-marked foliage shows green, purple, and variegated tones through the season, staying low and dense even as it colonizes broadly. Short spikes of small white flowers appear above the foliage in mid-spring. Keep soil evenly moist, especially the first year, to encourage the runners to establish and root at their nodes.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade and mulch to keep the shallow roots cool. Mint Chocolate is named for its unusually long, narrow, maple-shaped leaves, mint green overlaid with a bold, dark chocolate-brown band tracing the veins, a pattern that deepens into rich bronze tones through winter. In early spring, wiry stems carry toffee-tinted flower spikes just above the patterned foliage. The clumping habit spreads gently rather than aggressively, making it well suited to a shaded border edge or woodland path where its foliage color can be appreciated up close.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where the clump will spread by runners into a dense, foot-or-more-wide patch over a few seasons. Skeleton Key bears semi-glossy, deeply and intricately cut dark green leaves tinged with purple, giving the foliage an open, lacy, almost skeletal look distinct from broader-leaved foamflowers. Numerous wiry, erect stems carry tiny white star-shaped flowers for about six weeks in spring, creating a long-lasting foamy display above the foliage. Divide congested patches every few years in spring or fall to maintain vigor and control spread.
